items.readable_text:
Content:
When subtracting mixed numbers, we sometimes run into a problem when subtracting the fractional parts.

Content:
For example, let's try to work out the following problem:

Content:
[MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{6} - 2 \,\dfrac{1}{3}]

Content:
If we try to subtract fractions from fractions, we run into a problem:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{6} - \dfrac{1}{3}\quad \color{red}{\times}]

Content:
We cannot perform the above subtraction because [MATH: \dfrac 1 6 < \dfrac 1 3.]

Content:
To get around this problem, we convert each mixed number to an improper fraction, and then subtract.

Content:
Writing [MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{6}] as an improper fraction, we have:
[MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{(4 \times 6) + 1}{6} = \dfrac{25}{6}]

Content:
Writing [MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{1}{3}] as an improper fraction, we have:
[MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{(2 \times 3) + 1}{3} = \dfrac {7}{3}]

Content:
Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:
[MATH: \dfrac{25}{6} - \dfrac {7}{3}]

Content:
We can make a common denominator of [MATH: 6.] To put [MATH: \dfrac{7}{3}] over a denominator of [MATH: 6,] we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 2]:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{7}{3} = \dfrac{7 \times 2}{3 \times 2} = \dfrac{14}{6}]

Content:
We can now subtract the fractions:

Content:
[MATH: (25)/(6) − (14)/(6) = (11)/(6)]

sections.normalized_html:
Writing [MATH: 5 \, \dfrac{1}{9}] as an improper fraction, we have

[MATH: 5 \, \dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{(5 \times 9) + 1}{9} = \dfrac{46}{9} .]

Writing [MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{3}] as an improper fraction, we have

[MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{(4 \times 3) + 1}{3} = \dfrac{13}{3} .]

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

[MATH: \dfrac{46}{9} - \dfrac{13}{3}]

We can make a common denominator of [MATH: 9.] To put [MATH: \dfrac{13}{3}] over a denominator of [MATH: 9,] we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 3]:

[MATH: \dfrac{13}{3} = \dfrac{13 \times 3}{3 \times 3} = \dfrac{39}{9}]

We can now subtract the fractions.

[MATH: \dfrac{46}{9} - \dfrac{39}{9} = \dfrac{\bbox[2px,lightgray]{7}}{9}]

So the missing number is [MATH: 7.]

sections.normalized_html: By writing both mixed numbers as improper fractions, determine the value of [MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{4} - 2 \,\dfrac{1}{2}.]
sections.readable_text: By writing both mixed numbers as improper fractions, determine the value of [MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{4} - 2 \,\dfrac{1}{2}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Writing [MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{4}] as an improper fraction, we have

[MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{(4 \times 4) + 1}{4} = \dfrac{17}{4} .]

Writing [MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{1}{2}] as an improper fraction, we have

[MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{(2 \times 2) + 1}{2} = \dfrac {5}{2} .]

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

[MATH: \dfrac{17}{4} - \dfrac {5}{2}]

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of [MATH: 4.]

To put [MATH: \dfrac{5}{2}] over a denominator of [MATH: 4,] we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 2]:

[MATH: \dfrac{5}{2} = \dfrac{5 \times 2}{2 \times 2} = \dfrac{10}{4}]

We can now subtract the fractions.

[MATH: (17)/(4) − (10)/(4) = (7)/(4)]

items.title: Converting the Result to a Mixed Number

sections.normalized_html: By writing both mixed numbers as improper fractions, express [MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{8} - 1 \,\dfrac{1}{4}] as a mixed number.
sections.readable_text: By writing both mixed numbers as improper fractions, express [MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{8} - 1 \,\dfrac{1}{4}] as a mixed number.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If we attempt to subtract the fractions by putting them over a common denominator, we get the following: [MATH: (1)/(8) − (1)/(4)|= (1)/(8) − (2 × 1)/(2 × 4); = (1)/(8) − (2)/(8)]

However, we cannot carry out this subtraction since the first fraction is smaller than the second!

To get around this problem, we write each mixed number as an improper fraction.

  • Writing [MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{8}] as an improper fraction, we have [MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{(3 \times 8) + 1}{8} = \dfrac{25}{8} .]

  • Writing [MATH: 1 \, \dfrac{1}{4}] as an improper fraction, we have [MATH: 1 \, \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{(1 \times 4) + 1}{4} = \dfrac{5}{4} .]

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

[MATH: \dfrac{25}{8} - \dfrac{5}{4}]

We can make a common denominator of [MATH: 8.] To put [MATH: \dfrac{5}{4}] over a denominator of [MATH: 8,] we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 2\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: \dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{5 \times 2}{4 \times 2} = \dfrac{10}{8}]

We can now subtract the fractions:

[MATH: \dfrac{25}{8} - \dfrac{10}{8} = \dfrac{15}{8}]

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

[MATH: \dfrac{15}{8} = 1 \, \textrm{R} \, 7 = 1 \, \dfrac{7}{8}]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When subtracting mixed numbers, we sometimes run into a problem when subtracting the fractional parts.

Content:
For example, let's try to work out the following problem:

Content:
[MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{6} - 2 \,\dfrac{1}{3}]

Content:
If we try to subtract fractions from fractions, we run into a problem:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{6} - \dfrac{1}{3}\quad \color{red}{\times}]

Content:
We cannot perform the above subtraction because [MATH: \dfrac 1 6 < \dfrac 1 3.]

Content:
To get around this problem, we convert each mixed number to an improper fraction, and then subtract.

Content:
Writing [MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{6}] as an improper fraction, we have:
[MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{(4 \times 6) + 1}{6} = \dfrac{25}{6}]

Content:
Writing [MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{1}{3}] as an improper fraction, we have:
[MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{(2 \times 3) + 1}{3} = \dfrac {7}{3}]

Content:
Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:
[MATH: \dfrac{25}{6} - \dfrac {7}{3}]

Content:
We can make a common denominator of [MATH: 6.] To put [MATH: \dfrac{7}{3}] over a denominator of [MATH: 6,] we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 2]:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{7}{3} = \dfrac{7 \times 2}{3 \times 2} = \dfrac{14}{6}]

Content:
We can now subtract the fractions:

Content:
[MATH: (25)/(6) − (14)/(6) = (11)/(6)]

Writing [MATH: 5 \, \dfrac{1}{9}] as an improper fraction, we have

[MATH: 5 \, \dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{(5 \times 9) + 1}{9} = \dfrac{46}{9} .]

Writing [MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{3}] as an improper fraction, we have

[MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{(4 \times 3) + 1}{3} = \dfrac{13}{3} .]

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

[MATH: \dfrac{46}{9} - \dfrac{13}{3}]

We can make a common denominator of [MATH: 9.] To put [MATH: \dfrac{13}{3}] over a denominator of [MATH: 9,] we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 3]:

[MATH: \dfrac{13}{3} = \dfrac{13 \times 3}{3 \times 3} = \dfrac{39}{9}]

We can now subtract the fractions.

[MATH: \dfrac{46}{9} - \dfrac{39}{9} = \dfrac{\bbox[2px,lightgray]{7}}{9}]

So the missing number is [MATH: 7.]

Item 5 — Example: Subtracting Mixed Numbers Using Improper Fractions

Example Prompt:
By writing both mixed numbers as improper fractions, determine the value of [MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{4} - 2 \,\dfrac{1}{2}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Writing [MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{4}] as an improper fraction, we have

[MATH: 4 \, \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{(4 \times 4) + 1}{4} = \dfrac{17}{4} .]

Writing [MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{1}{2}] as an improper fraction, we have

[MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{(2 \times 2) + 1}{2} = \dfrac {5}{2} .]

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

[MATH: \dfrac{17}{4} - \dfrac {5}{2}]

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of [MATH: 4.]

To put [MATH: \dfrac{5}{2}] over a denominator of [MATH: 4,] we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 2]:

[MATH: \dfrac{5}{2} = \dfrac{5 \times 2}{2 \times 2} = \dfrac{10}{4}]

We can now subtract the fractions.

[MATH: (17)/(4) − (10)/(4) = (7)/(4)]

[MATH: (1)/(8) − (1)/(4)|= (1)/(8) − (2 × 1)/(2 × 4); = (1)/(8) − (2)/(8)]

However, we cannot carry out this subtraction since the first fraction is smaller than the second!

To get around this problem, we write each mixed number as an improper fraction.

- Writing [MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{8}] as an improper fraction, we have
[MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{(3 \times 8) + 1}{8} = \dfrac{25}{8} .]
- Writing [MATH: 1 \, \dfrac{1}{4}] as an improper fraction, we have
[MATH: 1 \, \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{(1 \times 4) + 1}{4} = \dfrac{5}{4} .]

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

[MATH: \dfrac{25}{8} - \dfrac{5}{4}]

We can make a common denominator of [MATH: 8.] To put [MATH: \dfrac{5}{4}] over a denominator of [MATH: 8,] we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 2\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: \dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{5 \times 2}{4 \times 2} = \dfrac{10}{8}]

We can now subtract the fractions:

[MATH: \dfrac{25}{8} - \dfrac{10}{8} = \dfrac{15}{8}]

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:
